stimulus.text:
A historian argues: 'The arrival of enslaved Africans in Virginia in 1619 established race-based slavery in the British colonies, and the plantation slavery of the mid-1700s was essentially the same system that began in 1619.' Virginia's laws on slavery hardened step by step:

| Year | Law or case | What it did |
| 1640 | John Punch | A Black runaway and two white runaways were caught together; the white men got four more years added to their terms, while Punch was condemned to slavery for life. |
| 1655 | John Casor | A Northampton County court declared Casor, an African servant, a slave for life — the first civil-court ruling of its kind in the English colonies. |
| 1662 | Partus sequitur ventrem | A child's status followed the mother, so the children of enslaved women were born enslaved — breaking English common law, where status followed the father. |
| 1667 | Baptism | Virginia declared that baptism did not free an enslaved person. |
| 1705 | Slave code | Virginia gathered its slave laws into one code: 'All Negro, mulatto and Indian slaves within this dominion… shall be held to be real estate.' |
stimulus.source_note: Original table written for this question from Barron's 2027 Ch 4, 5 Steps 2024 Ch 8, and the Virginia slave code of 1705 (public domain). The Casor date follows the March 8, 1655 Northampton County ruling; Barron's dates the Casor case to 1640, which conflates it with the John Punch case of 1640.

source: original; stimulus is an original secondary passage written for this question

books.section: The Nature of Slavery in British North America

primary_sources: Johnson v. Parker, Northampton County court ruling (March 8, 1655)

stem: Virginia's comprehensive slave codes of 1705 defined enslaved people as property and stripped away legal rights. A historian argues these laws reveal as much about planters' fears as about their power. Which context best supports that interpretation?

options.text: The codes were copied directly from English laws governing London apprentices and servants.
options.misconception: No equivalent English laws governed apprentices as racial property.

options.text: The codes applied only to newly arrived Africans and exempted those born in Virginia.
options.misconception: The codes defined enslaved status broadly, including the children of enslaved mothers.

options.text: The codes were passed because slavery was becoming economically unimportant in the Chesapeake.
options.misconception: Slavery was becoming more, not less, central to the Chesapeake economy.

options.text: The codes followed decades of resistance, showing slavery required constant legal force.

rationales.general:
1. Read what the code did. It defined enslaved people as property and stripped away legal rights.
2. Ask why a government writes such a code. To hold a system together that people keep resisting.
3. Look at the timing. Background: the code came after Bacon's Rebellion and decades of resistance.
4. Name what the timing shows. Planters legislating from fear of a system that needed constant force.
Remember: a harsh law is evidence twice over — it shows the power claimed and the resistance feared.
rationales.D: The 1705 code came after Bacon's Rebellion and decades of resistance — runaways, conspiracies, and uprisings that planters had to answer with law. A code that defines people as property, restricts movement and assembly, and strips away legal rights is a government legislating from fear: the system needed constant force to hold together. That is why the laws reveal planters' fears as much as their power. The other options are wrong: the codes were Virginia's own, they covered enslaved children, and slavery was growing more central.
rationales.A: No equivalent English laws governed apprentices as racial property.
rationales.B: The codes defined enslaved status broadly, including the children of enslaved mothers.
rationales.C: Slavery was becoming more, not less, central to the Chesapeake economy.
